summary.title: Understanding Wi-Fi 4/5/6/6E/7/8 (802.11 n/ac/ax/be/bn)
summary.one_liner: Learn why real-world Wi-Fi speed is usually limited by your client device, distance, and MIMO/channel width rather than the router's advertised number, and how to estimate achievable throughput.
takeaways: Advertised aggregate router speeds (e.g. AC5300) add up all bands and are rarely reachable by a single client; the usable figure is the PHY rate for one band at the lowest common MIMO and channel width.
Client devices are usually the bottleneck: most phones, tablets and laptops are 2x2 MIMO, so a new router often will not speed them up.
Wi-Fi speed drops steeply with distance because higher QAM levels need a clean signal; being close to the access point matters most.
Estimate real application throughput by taking about 70% of the PHY rate, then confirm with speed tests.
Use a wired access point rather than a wireless range extender to improve coverage at distance.
summary.summary: This long-form reference explains how Wi-Fi works in the United States, covering generations from Wi-Fi 1 through Wi-Fi 7 and the 802.11 standards behind them. It uses tables of symbol rate, bits per symbol, QAM, MIMO, channel width and PHY speed, plus worked examples (such as an AC5300 router reduced to about 455 Mbps for a 2x2 client at 32 feet). It frames the main limits as client capability, distance, MAC overhead and contention, and ends with a method to estimate real throughput from the PHY rate. The page is updated regularly and includes recommendations and a glossary, though the excerpt provided is partial.
